rationale: A wins because it keeps four clean protagonists and makes the missing facts part of the story instead of wallpapering over them. Its best line, "Perplexity will pay publishers it cites. It won't say how much," is sharp, grounded, and immediately reportable. B has instincts, but "Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" drags in competitors the update never gave, and "publishers are already being cited in answers whether or not they join the program" is not in the facts. That is how a useful angle becomes a liability.
gaps_in_A: "takes a referral fee on every sale" overstates the update. The facts support referral fees on in-app purchases, not necessarily every sale or every recommendation.
"The launch is the first concrete monetization signal since the raise" is not supplied. It may be strategically plausible, but it needs verification before a VC reporter sees it.
"when you buy what it recommends" slightly outruns the wording. The update says users can research and buy products; it does not prove paid recommendations or ranking influence.
gaps_in_B: "Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" is an invented competitor frame. No competitor was in the update, and direct competition is a claim, not a vibe.
"for the first time, an AI search product is inserting itself into the transaction" is unsupported market-history swagger. If you cannot prove first, do not write first.
"publishers are already being cited in answers whether or not they join the program" and "content is cited regardless" are not in the facts. That is a serious grounding miss.
"Publishers Who Threatened Perplexity..." and "Perplexity Says It's Sharing Revenue..." are too close: same publisher conflict, same opacity hole, same proof burden. Keep the sharper one.
